plain: GitHub Copilot is a helper that lives inside the program where you write the instructions the computer is going to follow. As you type, it guesses how the sentence continues and shows it to you in gray, right where the cursor blinks. It's your phone's predictive text, except instead of finishing your word it finishes twenty lines in a row. And like the one on your phone, it gets it right a lot and gets it wrong with the same confident face.

account.free: Yes, there's a free plan. It's called Copilot Free and gives you about 2,000 autocomplete suggestions a month and about 50 chat messages: plenty for learning for weeks. If you run short, the Pro plan costs about 10 dollars a month, or about 100 dollars if you pay for the whole year, and removes the cap. If you're a student or teacher and verify your institution, Pro is free. Prices and caps change every few months: check the number shown today at github.com/features/copilot before entering your card.
steps: Go to github.com and click Sign up, top right. It asks for an email, a password, and a username. That name is public, and changing it later breaks any links you've already shared, so pick something you'd be fine showing in a job interview.

Download Visual Studio Code from code.visualstudio.com. The big blue button says Download for Windows. It's the program where you're going to write. Install it by clicking Next. It's free and won't ask for a card.

Inside Visual Studio Code, in the icon column on the left, click the one that looks like four little squares with one detached. It's called Extensions: things you plug into the editor so it can do something new. The keyboard shortcut is Ctrl+Shift+X.

In the search box type GitHub Copilot. It shows up first in the list, with the word Microsoft under the name. Click Install and wait a few seconds. If it also offers GitHub Copilot Chat, install it too: that's what gives you the inline chat, and you'll use it from day one.

A notice appears bottom right saying Sign in to use GitHub Copilot. Click it. The browser opens with a GitHub page that says Authorize Visual Studio Code. Read the permissions it's asking for, click the green button, and go back to the editor: the notice is gone.

In the gray bar at the very bottom there's a small Copilot icon. If it looks normal, it's working. If it has a diagonal bar over it, it's off: click it and choose Enable Completions. To test it, create a file, save it as test.py, write a line starting with a hash sign, and wait two seconds.
Set it to talk in English

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type settings json, and choose Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON), which is your preferences file. Inside it, add the line "github.copilot.chat.localeOverride": "en" and save with Ctrl+S. From then on the chat answers you in English even though the code stays in English too. You have the whole file, ready to paste, in the templates further down.
account.warning: Copilot doesn't guess out of nowhere: it reads the files you have open in the editor and sends them to its servers to calculate the suggestion. Don't leave a file open with passwords, ID numbers, client emails, or account numbers while it's turned on. And if you subscribe to Pro, it renews itself every month until you cancel it by hand at github.com/settings/billing. Nobody warns you the day before.

first: Create a new file and save it with a name and extension, for example invoices.py. If you don't save it, Copilot doesn't know what language you're writing in and suggests random things.
Write a short sentence explaining what you want, starting with the language's comment symbol. In Python that's the hash sign: # calculate the price with 21 percent tax.
Press Enter and wait a second or two without touching anything. Light gray text appears. That's the proposal, it doesn't exist yet.
Read it all, top to bottom, numbers included. Only then decide: Tab accepts it whole, Esc throws it away.

Select with the mouse what you just accepted and press Ctrl+I. A little box opens over the code: type explain this to me in plain English, line by line. That's the inline chat and it's your translator.
Deliberately discard three suggestions that looked good to you. Sounds silly, but it's the muscle that saves you later: making Tab a decision, not a reflex.
shortcuts: Tab

Accepts the ENTIRE gray suggestion. Not the line you're looking at: the whole block, whether it's 2 lines or 25. It's the shortcut you'll use the most, and the only one that can slip in an error that doesn't throw an error.
Esc
Throws the gray suggestion away. It doesn't delete anything of yours, it just makes what didn't exist yet disappear. Use it guilt-free: you can always ask for it again.
Ctrl + right arrow

Accepts only the next WORD of the suggestion. It's the slow version of Tab and the one that teaches you to read: you feed the code in bit by bit, and as soon as something doesn't line up, you stop and press Esc.
Ctrl + Z

Undo. Your panic button after a Tab you regret. Press it several times in a row if needed; each press undoes one more step back. It works even after the file is saved, as long as you haven't closed the editor.
Ctrl + I

Opens the inline chat: a text box attached to wherever you are, right inside the code. You ask for something in English, it proposes the change painted in green and red, and you decide. It's the most honest way to work, because you see exactly what it touches.
Ctrl + Alt + I

Opens the side chat, the conversation column on the right. There you ask longer questions without touching the file. The one next to it, Ctrl+Shift+I, opens multi-file edit mode in newer versions: don't touch that yet.
Alt + ] and Alt + [

Shows the next and previous proposal, because there's almost never just one. Note: on some keyboard layouts the bracket keys need AltGr, so sometimes these two won't respond. Safe alternative: hold the mouse still over the gray text and a floating bar appears with < > arrows.
Alt + backslash

Asks for a suggestion by hand, without waiting. Useful when Copilot goes quiet because you've deleted and rewritten a lot. On some keyboard layouts the backslash needs a special combination, so you may need to search for the command in the palette.
Ctrl + Enter

Inside the inline chat, confirms the proposed changes. In the editor, in some versions, it opens a panel with up to ten proposals at once for you to choose from. It varies by the version you have installed: trust the button you see on screen (Accept / Discard) over the shortcut.
Ctrl + Shift + P

The command palette: a search bar that finds anything the editor knows how to do. Type copilot and every one of its commands shows up with its shortcut written next to it. It's the cheat sheet that never goes stale, the one you use when a shortcut doesn't respond.
daily: Always write a comment in English BEFORE waiting for the gray text. The quality of the suggestion depends almost entirely on the sentence above it: the more specific (names, units, what goes in and what comes out), the less junk it proposes.
Accept in pieces, not blocks. Ctrl+right arrow to go word by word when the code touches money, emails, deletions, or anything sent outside. Tab only once you've already read the entire lines.

Select a chunk and press Ctrl+I to ask for changes in plain language: do it in dollars, add 21% tax, warn if the field arrives empty. The inline chat works ON what you've selected, so selecting little is how you keep it touching little.
Run the program after each acceptance, not every twenty. If something breaks, you know exactly which line broke it because you just added it yourself.
Close tabs that aren't related to what you're doing. Copilot looks at open files for inspiration: if you have an old example open, it'll copy its quirks, its names, and its mistakes.

Always double-check three things in what you accept: the numbers (percentages, prices, limits), the text in quotes (emails, web addresses, file names), and any line starting with import or require, which is where it can slip in pieces you don't have installed.
When something smells off, Ctrl+Z first and ask questions later. Undoing is free; debugging code you didn't write and don't understand can eat your afternoon.

templates.name: Project instructions file (copilot-instructions.md)
templates.what: A rulesheet Copilot reads on its own every time you ask it something in chat, without you having to repeat it. It's for never having to type answer me in English, I don't know how to code, tax is 21% ever again. It's the first thing anyone vibecoding should create, because it turns the assistant into one that already knows your project.
templates.how: 1) In the editor's left column, with your project's folder open, click the new-folder icon and name it .github (yes, with the dot in front). 2) Inside it, new-file icon, and name it copilot-instructions.md. 3) Paste the text below and change what's in brackets. 4) Save with Ctrl+S. 5) Open the chat with Ctrl+Alt+I and ask anything: below its response a line appears saying Used 1 reference. Expand it and if it says copilot-instructions.md, it's working.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
What you call what you're building, even if it's one word
[ONE SENTENCE: WHO IT HELPS AND HOW]
Your idea in one line, the way you'd explain it to your mother
[CUSTOMERS / JUST ME / MY TEAM]
Who's actually going to use this, because it changes how much care is needed
The sales tax that applies to you; change it or make it a configurable value if it varies
templates.code:
# Instructions for GitHub Copilot on this project

## How to talk to me
- Always answer me in plain English.
- I don't know how to code. Before writing code, explain in two sentences what it's going to do.
- Translate every technical word the first time you use it.
- If something costs money, deletes data, or can't be undone, warn me in CAPITAL LETTERS before the code.

## What I'm building
- Project: [PROJECT NAME]
- What it's for: [ONE SENTENCE: WHO IT HELPS AND HOW]
- Who's going to use it: [CUSTOMERS / JUST ME / MY TEAM]

## Code rules
- Variable and function names in English; comments in English.
- No passwords, keys, or real emails inside the code: those go in a .env file.
- Money: dollars. Tax rate: 21%. Dates: MM/DD/YYYY.
- Don't add new libraries without telling me and explaining what each one is for.
- I prefer long, clear code over short and clever.
- Every function, a comment above it in English explaining what goes in and what comes out.

## What NOT to do
- Don't delete files or folders.
- Don't change anything I haven't asked for.
- Don't make up function names: if you're not sure they exist, say so.
- Don't give me four alternatives: give me the one you'd use, and why.

templates.name: VS Code settings for vibecoding
templates.what: The editor's preferences file, set up ready for someone who doesn't code: chat in English, suggestions turned off in plain text files (where they just get in the way), bigger font, autosave, and the arrow toolbar always visible over the gray text so you can switch proposals with the mouse.
templates.how: 1) Press Ctrl+Shift+P. 2) Type settings json and choose Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON). 3) A file with braces opens. If it's empty or has only {}, delete everything and paste this as-is. If you already had things in it, copy only the lines you're missing, and make sure each line ends with a comma except the last. 4) Save with Ctrl+S. 5) If red underlines appear, it's an extra or missing comma: Ctrl+Z and try again.
fill: "editor.fontSize": 15
Bump it to 17 or 18 if it strains your eyes; it doesn't break anything
"files.autoSaveDelay": 1000
Milliseconds it waits before autosaving. 1000 is one second
"github.copilot.enable"
Add any file type where you don't want suggestions, set to false
templates.code:
{
  "github.copilot.chat.localeOverride": "en",
  "github.copilot.enable": {
    "*": true,
    "plaintext": false,
    "markdown": true
  },
  "editor.inlineSuggest.enabled": true,
  "editor.inlineSuggest.showToolbar": "always",
  "editor.fontSize": 15,
  "editor.wordWrap": "on",
  "editor.renderWhitespace": "boundary",
  "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
  "files.autoSaveDelay": 1000,
  "explorer.confirmDelete": true,
  "workbench.editor.enablePreview": false
}

templates.name: Shortcuts to accept line by line (keybindings.json)
templates.what: Four new shortcuts that let you feed in the suggestion piece by piece instead of swallowing it whole with Tab: a word, a line, and switching proposals without fighting bracket keys on some layouts. It's the safety net of this whole document, turned into keys.
templates.how: 1) Ctrl+Shift+P. 2) Type keyboard shortcuts json and choose Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON). 3) Paste the block below inside the brackets already there, or paste the whole file if it was empty. 4) Ctrl+S. 5) Test it: write a comment, wait for the gray text, and press Ctrl+Alt+right arrow. A single word should get typed in. If a shortcut does nothing, your version doesn't have that command: open Ctrl+K Ctrl+S, search for inline suggest, and see which ones actually exist in your install. Nothing bad happens, that one just doesn't work.
fill: "ctrl+alt+right"
Change it if you already use it for something else; any free combination works
"ctrl+alt+down"
This is the important one: accepts one line and stops

templates.name: Leak shield (.gitignore and .env.example)
templates.what: Two files that prevent this course's most expensive mistake: uploading a password Copilot suggested to the internet. The .gitignore is a list of things that never get uploaded. The .env is where the real keys live, on your computer and only there. The .env.example is the fake copy, with empty placeholders, so people can see what keys are needed without revealing any of them.
templates.how: 1) In your project's root folder, create a file called .gitignore (with the dot in front and no extension) and paste the first part of the code. 2) Create another called .env.example and paste the second part. 3) Create a third called .env, copy the same content as the example into it, and this time write your real keys. 4) Confirm it's working: in the left column, the name .env should show up dimmed gray. If it looks the same as the others, .gitignore isn't catching it. WARNING: this needs to be done BEFORE uploading the project for the first time. A key you've already uploaded doesn't get removed by deleting it: it stays in the history, and there are automated programs scanning GitHub specifically to find them.
fill: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
Only if you take payments with Stripe; if not, delete it
DATABASE_URL
Your database's address, if you have one
EMAIL_PASSWORD
The password for the email account you send from, never your personal one
templates.code:
# ---------- File 1: .gitignore ----------
# Everything listed here NEVER gets uploaded to the internet.
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
secrets/
*.key
*.pem

# System and tooling clutter
node_modules/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.log
*.sqlite
*.db
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db


# ---------- File 2: .env.example ----------
# Copy this file, call it .env, and fill in the real values there.
# This example one is deliberately empty: it gets uploaded, and shouldn't reveal anything.
OPENAI_API_KEY=
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=
DATABASE_URL=
EMAIL_PASSWORD=
APP_ENV=development

errors: Sign in to use GitHub Copilot

Notice bottom right: you're not signed in, or the session expired (happens every few weeks, or if you switch networks). Click the notice, authorize in the browser, and go back to the editor. If the browser stays blank, close VS Code completely and reopen it.
GitHub Copilot could not connect to server. Extension activation failed: "getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND"

It can't reach the servers. It's almost always your connection, an active VPN, or an office wifi that blocks it. Try opening github.com in the browser: if that doesn't load either, it's the network. Copilot doesn't work offline, it doesn't save anything for later.
You have exceeded your monthly completions limit / Upgrade to Copilot Pro

You've used up this month's free plan quota. The exact wording changes with versions, but it always mentions limit and Upgrade. Two options: wait until the 1st of next month, or pay about 10 dollars a month. To be clear: clicking Upgrade signs you up for something that renews itself until you cancel it at github.com/settings/billing.
The Copilot icon bottom right has a diagonal bar over it

It's turned off, either entirely or just for this file type. Click the icon: a menu shows up with Enable Completions and the option to enable it only for the language you're currently in. If you turned it off by accident with a shortcut, this is where you turn it back on.

Copilot wrote you code that uses a piece you don't have installed. It imagined it was available because in the projects it learned from, it was. Fix: open the terminal with Ctrl+` (or View > Terminal) and run pip install requests, swapping requests for the name shown in quotes. If the name doesn't exist anywhere, it made it up entirely: delete it and ask again, telling it to use only standard libraries.
IndentationError: unexpected indent  /  SyntaxError: invalid syntax

You accepted a suggestion on top of code that was already there, and now pieces are stuck together or misaligned. Don't try to fix it by hand at first: Ctrl+Z several times until the file is back to how it was, and try again with the cursor on an empty line.
Sorry, your request failed. Please try again. Request id: 8f2c…

The chat failed on its end, not yours. Resend the same message. If it fails three times in a row, check githubstatus.com: when there's an outage, it shows up there before anywhere else. Don't rewrite your project thinking it's your fault.
Copilot doesn't suggest anything, no gray text and no warning, in a newly created file

Almost always the file isn't saved and has no extension, so the editor doesn't know what language it is. Save it with Ctrl+S giving it .py, .html, or whatever fits. Look bottom right: it shows the detected language's name. If it says Plain Text, that's the problem.

prompts.name: Review a block you already accepted without understanding it
prompts.prompt: Act as a code reviewer explaining things to someone who doesn't code and never will. I'm handing you a block you wrote for me that I accepted with Tab without fully understanding it. The project is [WHAT YOU'RE BUILDING, ONE SENTENCE] and this piece is supposed to [WHAT YOU THINK THIS CODE DOES]. Answer me in plain English, and do these four things in this exact order. First: tell me in five sentences, with no untranslated technical word, what this code actually does, grouping the lines into blocks. Second: tell me if it does anything I did NOT ask for, specifically connecting to the internet, deleting or overwriting files, saving data to disk, or sending information outside my computer, and point me to the exact line and line number. Third: check every number, every text in quotes, every web address, and every file name, and tell me which ones you made up or copied from a generic example; I especially care about the tax percentage, which here is [21], and the currency, which is [dollars]. Fourth: tell me what happens if I feed it weird input, meaning an empty field, text where you expected a number, zero, a negative number, and a huge number. End with a single final line that says USE IT or DON'T USE IT and why, in ten words. Don't rewrite the code yet: today I just want to know what's wrong with it.

prompts.name: Plan first, code after (so you don't accept blindly)
prompts.prompt: I want to build [DESCRIBE YOUR IDEA IN TWO OR THREE SENTENCES: WHAT IT IS, WHO IT'S FOR, WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN WHEN SOMEONE USES IT]. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: I'll ask you for things in English, you write the code, and I test it. Before writing a single line, I want a plan. Give me, in plain English: one, the list of files the project will have, with one sentence per file explaining what it does, as if you were explaining the drawers of a cabinet. Two, the order to build them in, starting with the smallest piece that can already be tested and seen working on screen; I want to see something alive at step one, not step eight. Three, for each step, how I check with my own eyes that it came out right: what I open, what I type, what I should see. Four, what's going to cost me money and how much per month in dollars, if anything does, and what free alternative exists. Five, which of the decisions you're making would be hard to change a month from now. Write it all in plain language, translating every technical word the first time. When you finish the plan, stop and wait for me to tell you where to start. Don't give me code in this response.

prompts.name: Sweep for passwords and personal data before uploading anything
prompts.prompt: You're going to act as a security auditor with me, and I can't read code, so be literal and boring. Review this project's files and find me five specific things. One: any password, access key, token, or long string of letters and numbers that looks like a credential, wherever it is, comments and examples you wrote yourself included. Two: emails, phone numbers, ID numbers, mailing addresses, or real people's names. Three: internal, testing, or my-own-machine web addresses, like localhost or an IP. Four: keys that look like they're from a payment service, especially ones starting with sk_, pk_, ghp_, or similar. Five: files that should never be uploaded to the internet, like .env, databases, or backups. For each finding, tell me: the file, the line number, what it is in plain language, how serious it is from 1 to 5, and exactly what to do to remove it, with numbered steps. At the end, write me the complete content of a .gitignore file adapted to this project, ready to copy. Answer me in plain English. If you find nothing, say so clearly instead of inventing findings to look good. Context: [WHERE YOU'RE GOING TO UPLOAD IT: PUBLIC GITHUB, PRIVATE, A SERVER].

prompts.name: Fix an error by understanding what happened
prompts.prompt: I got an error and I need to fix it, but more than that I need to understand why it happened, because otherwise it'll happen again tomorrow. This is the message exactly as it shows up, copied in full: [PASTE THE COMPLETE ERROR HERE, ALL THE LINES, EVEN IF THEY LOOK REPEATED]. What I was doing right before was: [WHAT YOU DID: I ACCEPTED A SUGGESTION, I CLICKED RUN, I SAVED THE FILE]. The last thing I changed in the project was: [WHAT YOU LAST TOUCHED]. Answer me in plain English and in this order. One: translate the error message into a normal-person sentence, no jargon, starting with what the computer expected and didn't find. Two: tell me which file and which line the problem is in, and if it's the fault of a line you wrote for me, say so plainly. Three: give me the fix, but show me only the lines that change, with a before and after, not the whole file. Four: explain what sign I could have noticed to catch it before running it. Five: tell me if this fix could break something else in the project, and what. If you need to see a file you don't have in front of you, ask me for it by name instead of assuming what's in it.

words: Code editor
The program where you write the instructions the computer is going to follow. From the outside it looks like a black word processor; on the inside it warns you when you get them wrong.
Extension
An add-on you plug into the editor so it can do something it couldn't before. Like adding a roof rack to a car: same car, now it carries more.
Autocomplete
The program guessing the rest of what you're typing and offering it to you before you type it yourself.
Gray suggestion
The faint text that appears ahead of the blinking cursor. It's not really written: move to another line and it vanishes without a trace.
Tab
The tab key, the one with two arrows above the caps lock key. Here it means one thing: I accept everything in gray, as-is, down to the last line.
Inline chat

A conversation box that opens right inside the code, at the spot where you are, with Ctrl+I. You talk to it in English and it proposes the change right there, green for what's added and red for what's removed, with two buttons: Accept and Discard.
Accept and discard
The two only decisions you make all day. Accept puts the text into your actual file. Discard makes it disappear without touching anything of yours. Discard never breaks anything; accept can.
Keyboard shortcut
A key combination that does the same thing as hunting through a menu, but in half a second. The ones in this document all show up next to their name if you press Ctrl+Shift+P.
Comment
A sentence you write for people to read. The computer skips it when running. Copilot, on the other hand, reads it very carefully: it's the easiest way to ask it for something.
Fabrication

When Copilot pulls a name, a piece, or a command out of thin air because it fits the rhythm of what you've written, even though it doesn't exist. It's not lying on purpose: its job is to sound right, not to be true.
matters: Read the whole suggestion before touching Tab. Tab doesn't accept the line you're looking at: it accepts the entire block, and sometimes that's 25 lines. The classic mistake is a number: you ask for 21 percent tax and it slips in 0.16 because the public projects it learned from used a different rate. That doesn't throw an error, it gives a result. You find out when the client tells you the invoice doesn't add up. If you're not going to read it, don't accept it: use Ctrl+right arrow and feed it in word by word.

Copilot doesn't run anything, so it doesn't know if it works. It hasn't tested its own proposal even once. If you accept twenty suggestions in a row without running the program, by the time it finally fails you'll have two hundred lines you haven't read and no clue where the problem is. Run it after every acceptance: it's the difference between a two-minute scare and a lost afternoon.

Never leave a password or access key written in the code, even if it suggests it. Copilot has learned from millions of public projects and sometimes spits out keys that look real, because they were. If that line ends up uploaded to the internet, it stays saved forever in the project's history: deleting it tomorrow doesn't remove it from today's version, and there are bots scanning GitHub to find them within minutes. That has no undo.

Go once to github.com/settings/copilot and check two boxes. One filters out suggestions that match public code word for word, so it doesn't slip you someone else's text. The other decides whether what you write is used for training. They come set however they come, and nobody's going to walk you there by hand.
ignore: The dropdown that lets you choose between several different brains. For gray autocomplete, the default one is fast and sharp. Changing it is a setting that'll make sense once you can actually tell the difference.

Agent mode and multi-file editing at once (Ctrl+Shift+I in newer versions). It's a different way of working, not an upgraded version of this one, and it accepts changes in files you don't even have open. Master the gray text, Tab, and Ctrl+I first: that's what gives you the judgment to evaluate the rest.

Fine-grained shortcuts, like opening a panel with ten proposals at once or fighting with Alt+bracket on some keyboard layouts. With Tab, Esc, Ctrl+right arrow, Ctrl+Z, and Ctrl+I you have more than enough for the first hundred hours.

questions.prompt: You're writing your first real program: getting the price with tax from a list of invoices. You write the comment, go down a line, and Copilot hands you 9 lines in gray. You look at the first one, it looks good and even uses the name you'd chosen. And you're in a hurry.

options.text: You scan down all 9 lines, confirm the multiplier is 1.21 and not something else, and only then press Tab.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is in the number. Tab accepts all 9 lines at once, not just the one you're looking at, so checking only the first line protects you from nothing. And the expensive mistake almost never crashes the program: it's a believable figure, a 1.16 or a 1.10, that gives a result and gets it wrong.

options.text: You press Tab and run the program to see if it breaks. If it works, it must be fine.
options.why: Anyone would think this, because testing things is a good instinct and it almost holds up here. It breaks in two places. One: a wrong percentage never crashes anything, it calmly returns a number. Two: at this pace, in half an hour you'll have 200 lines accepted and unread, and when something does fail you won't know where to look because you didn't write any of it.

options.text: You press Esc and type it all out by hand, since that's what you're learning to do and you don't trust it.
options.why: It's honest, and some days call for it, but it misreads the problem. The danger isn't that the suggestion exists, it's accepting it without looking. Reject everything on principle and you lose half the tool, and above all you never train the one skill that actually matters: reading code you didn't write and spotting what's off.

questions.explain: Tab doesn't accept one line: it signs off on the whole block. Read it before you sign.

questions.prompt: You're setting up a database connection. You type password = and Copilot fills in admin123 on its own. You test it and it connects perfectly. Tonight you're going to upload the project to GitHub to show a friend.

options.text: You delete that line, save the password in a separate config file, and make sure that file doesn't get uploaded.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is the order: fix it BEFORE uploading, not after. The moment you upload the project, the history keeps every previous version of the file. Deleting the password tomorrow doesn't remove it from today's version: it's still there for anyone looking, and there are automated programs scanning GitHub specifically for that. It's one of the few things in this course with no undo.

options.text: You leave it, you'll swap it for the real one once this becomes something serious.
options.why: This is what almost everyone does the first time, and it's understandable: it works, you're in a hurry, and it's not an important project yet. It breaks exactly at the moment you upload it. From then on that line isn't yours anymore, it lives in a public history that doesn't clean up by deleting the file. And note: admin123 wasn't invented by Copilot, it copied it from thousands of places where it was the real one.

options.text: You swap it for a long, hard password and leave it written in the file.
options.why: It sounds responsible, and it looks like it too. But the problem was never the password's strength, it was where it's written. A 40-character password published on the internet is exactly as useless as admin123: anyone can copy and paste it.

questions.explain: What you upload to the internet doesn't un-upload. The password comes out of the code before the first push, not after the first scare.

questions.prompt: You ask the inline chat (Ctrl+I) to add a 10% discount to the checkout page. It proposes the change: a green block and a red block appear, with two buttons below, Accept and Discard. The red block includes three lines you never asked it to touch.

options.text: You click Discard, and ask again after first selecting only the two price lines.
options.why: Correct. The inline chat works on what you have selected: select nothing and it takes liberties with the whole file. Discarding breaks nothing, it's free, and asking again with less text selected is how you keep it touching less. Red is what gets deleted: if there's something in there you don't understand, you're not ready to accept yet.

options.text: You click Accept, because the discount is done right and you'll look at the rest later.
options.why: This is the tool's expensive trap, and it's easy to fall into because the green part does exactly what you asked. The red part disappears from your file in that same click. It could be a stock warning, a check that the cart isn't empty, or the line that added tax. And since the program keeps working, you won't find out today.

options.text: You accept and then press Ctrl+Z if something goes wrong.
options.why: Ctrl+Z does save you, and it's a good reflex to have ready, but only if you notice within the next few seconds. The problem with accepting without reading is precisely that you notice nothing: no error, no warning, the page loads all the same. By the time you discover that check was missing, you'll have made twenty more changes on top, and undoing won't be a clean option anymore.

questions.explain: In the inline chat, green is what comes in and red is what leaves. What should worry you is the red.
